name: ʿAbd Allāh ibn Abī Isḥāq al-Ḥaḍramī
arabic: عَبْدُ اللهِ بْنُ أَبِي إِسْحَاقَ الحَضْرَمِيُّ
summary: The Basran whom the sources call the first to extend naḥw, stretch its analogy (qiyās) and set out its causes (ʿilal); he corrected the poets by the rules, and al-Farazdaq satirised him for it.
bio: Ibn Abī Isḥāq was a client of the family of al-Ḥaḍramī in Basra and learnt from Maymūn al-Aqran, a student of Abū al-Aswad's circle. Al-Zubaydī, after Ibn Sallām, calls him 'the first to open up naḥw, stretch analogy and explain the causes', and says he leant towards analogy. Yūnus ibn Ḥabīb, asked about his learning, said that he and the sea were the same.

He is the first grammarian of whom the sources tell that he judged the Arabs' own speech by the rules. Al-Zubaydī reports that he faulted a rhyme of the poet al-Farazdaq in a praise of the caliph Yazīd ibn ʿAbd al-Malik (the line ending mukhkhuhā rīru, which analogy wanted otherwise), that al-Farazdaq changed the line and people went back to the first version, and that the poet answered him with a satire: 'Were ʿAbd Allāh a client, I would satirise him; but ʿAbd Allāh is a client of clients.' A debate on the hamza before the governor Bilāl ibn Abī Burda he won against Abū ʿAmr ibn al-ʿAlāʾ, who then studied it closely. He also read some verses of the Qurʾān in a way of his own, which al-Zubaydī notes is not how the readers read them. He died in 117/735.
reception: His pupil ʿĪsā ibn ʿUmar carried his method on, and al-Khalīl learnt from ʿĪsā: the line of analogy in Basran grammar is traced through him.
